critiques.issue: The tree is empty, so I can't attack any conclusion. Nothing has been claimed, supported or refuted. The real risk is that the loop starts tuning before it has any structure, and later results get explained after the fact instead of checked against predictions.
critiques.suggestion: Before the second experiment, register 3–4 Lvl1 claims covering the two factors in time-to-75%. (a) Throughput: seconds per epoch, set by precision, compile, memory format and the data pipeline. (b) Sample efficiency: epochs needed to reach 75.3%, set by architecture, schedule, augmentation and loss. (c) Fixed overhead: prepare time, data loading to GPU, warmup that falls inside the timed region. (d) Accuracy variance, which sets how much margin above 0.753 is needed. Give each Lvl3 a numeric prediction (for example: 'bf16 + channels_last cuts epoch time by ≥30% with accuracy change within ±0.3pp').

critiques.issue: No experiment has run, so there is no reference time, accuracy or per-seed spread. Without a noise estimate, every later 'improvement' smaller than the noise is uninterpretable.
critiques.suggestion: Exp 1 should be the unmodified submission_template, run as-is. Record the per-seed accuracies and the per-trial prepare/train time split, not just the means. Use the seed spread to set a minimum effect size: with 3 seeds, a mean shift under about 2×(per-seed std)/√3 is noise. If the template is already infeasible, write down the gap to 0.753 explicitly.

critiques.issue: The constraint is a 3-seed mean ≥ 0.753, while judging uses 40 seeds at ≥ 0.75. A recipe tuned until it just clears 0.753 on seeds 0–2 is overfit to those fixed seeds. The 0.753 margin is only safe if per-seed std is about 0.3pp or less. Timing is also noisy (compile caching, GPU clocks, CPU contention on 4 cores), and the score is time.
critiques.suggestion: Add a Lvl1 on variance. Predict the per-seed std and check it by repeating the best config once, or by rerunning a key config. Don't accept a 'faster' result whose time gain is under about 2–3% without a repeat. Also don't accept a feasible result whose accuracy is under about 0.755 without a repeat.

critiques.target: Prior directions likely to be under-explored
critiques.issue: A few things specific to this task are easy to miss. (1) Test-time augmentation is banned, so recipes in the style of airbench that rely on flip-TTA lose about 0.5–1pp and need more training to make up for it. (2) Only 4 CPU cores are available, so a CPU DataLoader with torchvision transforms will likely bottleneck an A100. (3) prepare is timed, so moving the dataset to GPU and normalizing it counts against the score. (4) Compile, autotune and warmup are free in build, but only on synthetic data.
critiques.suggestion: Write the following as explicit Lvl2s. Load the whole uint8 dataset onto the GPU once in prepare, and do flip and crop augmentation on the GPU in batches. Run torch.compile with max-autotune plus a warmup in build. Use bf16 autocast with channels_last. Use a short schedule (one-cycle or linear decay), label smoothing, and an EMA or Lookahead whose state is reset in prepare. Scale the network up from a ResNet-9/airbench-style net: CIFAR-100 at 75% likely needs noticeably more width or epochs than CIFAR-10 at 94%.

critiques.target: Rule-compliance risk (not a hypothesis, but a failure mode)
critiques.issue: Speed tricks are where violations hide. Examples: state left over from warmup in build (BN running stats, optimizer moments, the RNG), any real data touched in build, and eval that changes state (BN in train mode) or runs over 5 s at B=1024 with an un-compiled shape. Any of these silently makes the best result invalid.
critiques.suggestion: Make 'the recipe is rule-compliant' a standing check on every feasible run. Confirm that prepare re-initializes params, buffers, optimizer, scheduler, EMA and RNG. Confirm that eval runs in eval mode under no_grad and works for B=1 and B=1024 (dynamic shapes or a fallback path).
